questions.q: Define 'non-human resources' as per NCERT Class 11 Home Science, and give two examples each of money and material goods.
questions.a: Non-human resources are tangible, external assets comprising money (medium of exchange) and material goods (physical objects like furniture, clothing, food, equipment). Examples of money: cash in hand, bank balance. Examples of material goods: dining table, school uniforms, LPG cylinder, textbooks. A wrong answer that lists "time" or "skills" reveals confusion between human and non-human resources — the student has not internalised that non-human resources are external and tangible, not personal attributes.

questions.q: Explain why money is described as a 'limited resource' in the textbook, and how this differs from the limitation of time as a human resource.
questions.a: Money is limited because its quantity is finite and unequally distributed across families — some have surplus, others barely meet needs — and it cannot be increased without earning. Time is limited differently: every person gets exactly 24 hours daily (equal distribution), but it cannot be saved, stored, or earned; once spent, it is gone forever. A wrong answer that says "both are limited so they are the same" misses the critical distinction: money's limitation is quantitative and unequal; time's limitation is universal and non-renewable.

questions.q: A family has ₹10,000 in savings, a functioning washing machine, and 50 sq. ft. of unused balcony space. They need to wash clothes daily, dry them, and save for a medical emergency. Apply the concept of interchangeability to propose two different ways they could meet the washing and drying needs without buying a new appliance.
questions.a: Option 1: Use the washing machine (material good) for washing; use balcony space (material good) for sun-drying — substituting a dryer (which they don't have) with free space and sunlight. Option 2: Hand-wash clothes (substituting machine with human energy — a human resource) to save machine wear and electricity cost (saving money), and use balcony for drying. A wrong answer that only says "use the washing machine" fails to demonstrate interchangeability — the student must show how one resource substitutes for another across categories (material for material, or human for material).

questions.q: Compare the accessibility of money versus material goods for a family living in a remote village versus an urban apartment. Analyse how location changes the accessibility of each resource type.
questions.a: In a remote village: money accessibility is lower (fewer ATMs/banks, irregular income from agriculture); material goods accessibility is mixed — space and firewood may be abundant (high accessibility), but specialised goods (medicines, branded stationery) require travel (low accessibility). In an urban apartment: money accessibility is higher (salaried income, digital banking, ATMs nearby); material goods accessibility is high for purchasable items but space is scarce and expensive (low accessibility for space). A wrong answer that says "money is equally accessible everywhere" ignores the textbook's explicit statement that accessibility varies by person, place, and time.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Since material goods can be substituted by money (you can buy anything), money is the only non-human resource that matters." Use the characteristics of utility and manageability to justify your position.
questions.a: The statement is flawed. Utility is goal- and situation-specific: during a power outage, a charged power bank (material good) has higher utility than ₹500 cash if shops are closed. Manageability requires using resources for maximum output with minimum input: buying ready-made meals daily (using only money) costs ₹3,000/month; cooking at home using utensils, stove, groceries (material goods) + human energy costs ₹1,500/month — the latter manages material goods better. A wrong answer that agrees with the statement ignores that material goods provide direct utility without transaction costs and can be managed to reduce monetary expenditure.

questions.q: Create a 'resource inventory table' for a Class 11 student preparing for board exams. List at least 5 non-human resources (money and material goods) they might have, and for each, specify its utility, current accessibility, one possible substitute, and how it can be managed for optimum use.
questions.a: Example row: Resource: Study table (material good) | Utility: Provides dedicated posture for long study sessions | Accessibility: High (already in room) | Substitute: Dining table / floor with cushion | Management: Keep clutter-free, position near natural light to reduce eye strain, use drawers for organised stationery access. A poor answer lists only "books, money, phone" without analysing each through the four characteristics — revealing the student cannot operationalise the framework for planning.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Non-human resources are tangible, external assets that individuals or families possess and utilise to achieve goals, comprising money (a universally accepted medium of exchange with limited ______ and unequal distribution) and material goods (physical objects such as space, furniture, clothing, stationery, food items, and equipment that have utility in performing activities).
Fill in the blank: Imagine your family has ₹5,000 saved for Diwali celebrations, but the ______ runs out, the geyser leaks, and your sibling needs new school shoes — all in the same week.
What is Non-human resources? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Non-human resources are tangible, external assets that individuals or families possess and utilise to achieve goals, comprising money (a universally accepted medium of exchange with limited availability and unequal distribution) and material goods (physical objects such as space, furniture, clothing, stationery, food items, and equipment.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Non-human resources?
questions.a: Students believe that "money can buy anything, so material goods are just a subset of money" — treating material goods as irrelevant once money is available.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) distinguish money and material goods as non-human resources with precise definitions and examples, (2) explain how the four characteristics of resources (utility, accessibility, interchangeability, manageability) apply specifically to money and material goods, and (3) analyse a real-life family scenario.
